summary: Sirach 22 begins with sharp comparisons for laziness, undisciplined children, ill-timed speech, and the difficulty of teaching a fool. It then contrasts unstable fear with a heart strengthened by counsel, and turns to friendship: injuries can sometimes be repaired, but insult, arrogance, betrayal, and disclosed secrets can make a friend flee. The chapter ends as a prayer for guarded speech so that the speaker's own tongue will not destroy him.
whyItMatters: This chapter sits in Sirach's larger instruction about ordinary conduct, especially speech, teachability, friendship, and disciplined judgment. It shows wisdom as practical formation in timing, counsel, loyalty, and restraint.

context.author: Yeshua, or Jesus, son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; his unnamed grandson later translated the Hebrew work into Greek in Egypt.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews who wanted instruction for life according to the law.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC, likely around 180–175 BC; the Greek translation followed after the grandson came to Egypt, commonly dated to 132 BC.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, scribal study, and Greek-speaking Mediterranean culture in the background.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction in compact poetic sayings, vivid comparisons, direct counsel, and prayer.

outline.heading: Sloth and Household Disgrace
outline.note: The chapter opens with harsh images for a slothful man and then turns to the shame or prudence associated with children, especially daughters, in an ancient household setting.

outline.heading: Bad Timing and the Fool
outline.note: Ill-timed conversation is compared to music in mourning, and teaching a fool is pictured as futile or barely received.

outline.heading: Missing Lines in This Edition
outline.note: The World English Bible leaves verses 9 and 10 blank; wording and verse numbering vary across editions of Sirach.

outline.heading: The Burden of Folly
outline.note: The sayings compare mourning for the dead with the longer grief caused by a fool, and warn against prolonged company with a person without understanding.

outline.heading: Established or Fearful Hearts
outline.note: A heart grounded in counsel and thoughtful understanding is contrasted with a fearful heart that cannot stand.

outline.heading: Friendship Injured and Restored
outline.note: The chapter describes how words and actions can wound a friend, when reconciliation may still be possible, and what conduct makes friendship fail.

outline.heading: A Guarded Mouth
outline.note: The final verse becomes a prayer for a watch over the mouth and a seal on the lips so speech will not ruin the speaker.

keyVerses.text: Ill-timed conversation is like music in mourning, but stripes and correction are wisdom in every season.
keyVerses.why: This verse anchors the chapter's concern with timing, speech, and correction.

keyVerses.text: Don’t talk much with a foolish man, and don’t go to one who has no understanding. Beware of him, lest you have trouble and be defiled in his onslaught. Turn away from him, and you will find rest, and you won’t be wearied in his madness.
keyVerses.why: It gives the chapter's practical warning about close association with folly.

keyVerses.text: If you have opened your mouth against a friend, don’t be afraid, for there may be reconciliation, unless it is for insulting, arrogance, disclosing of a secret, or a treacherous blow— for these things any friend will flee.
keyVerses.why: This verse states both the possibility and the limits of repairing damaged friendship.

keyVerses.text: Who will set a watch over my mouth, and a seal of shrewdness upon my lips, that I may not fall from it, and that my tongue may not destroy me?
keyVerses.why: The closing prayer gathers the chapter's repeated concern that speech can harm relationships and the speaker.

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin with such severe images for a slothful man?
questions.answer: Verses 1-2 use public, unpleasant comparisons to show how disgraceful sloth is in this wisdom setting. The point is not a modern psychological profile of laziness, but a vivid warning that a slothful person becomes socially repellent and difficult to handle.

questions.question: How should readers handle the statements about daughters and family shame?
questions.answer: Verses 3-5 speak from an ancient household world in which a daughter's conduct is described in relation to father and husband. Readers should notice that social setting rather than disguise it as neutral modern advice. The chapter's concrete concern is family honor and grief, but its assumptions about gender and household authority are historically distant from many modern readers.

questions.question: What is meant by “Ill-timed conversation”?
questions.answer: In verse 6, speech can be wrong because of its timing, even before its content is examined. The comparison to music in mourning pictures something that may be acceptable in one setting but jarring in another. This fits Sirach's wider concern with disciplined judgment about the fitting moment.

questions.question: Does the chapter say teaching a fool is always useless?
questions.answer: Verses 7-8 portray teaching a fool as frustrating and ineffective, like repairing broken pottery or waking someone who does not truly attend. The saying is deliberately sharp, but it is a wisdom comparison, not a full theory of education. It warns that instruction requires receptivity.

questions.question: Why are verses 9 and 10 blank here?
questions.answer: The World English Bible leaves verses 9 and 10 blank. Sirach survives in different textual forms, and editions can differ in wording and verse numbering. Other editions may include additional lines or number the passage differently.

questions.question: Why does Sirach say the life of the fool is worse than death?
questions.answer: Verse 11 compares grief for the dead with grief over a fool, saying the dead have found rest while the fool lacks understanding. Verse 12 extends the contrast by saying mourning for a fool and an ungodly man lasts all life long. Readers may differ over how literally to take the comparison, but within the saying it stresses the lasting burden caused by entrenched folly.

questions.question: What kind of stability is praised in verses 16-18?
questions.answer: The chapter praises a heart established on well advised counsel and settled upon thoughtful understanding. These images contrast with fences exposed to wind and a fearful heart that cannot stand. Stability here comes from counsel and understanding, not from mere stubbornness.

questions.question: Can a broken friendship be repaired in this chapter?
questions.answer: Yes, verses 21-22 say there may be a way back after drawing a sword or opening one's mouth against a friend. But the same passage names actions that may make a friend flee: insulting, arrogance, disclosing a secret, or a treacherous blow. The chapter holds together hope for reconciliation and realism about severe betrayal.

questions.question: Why does the chapter end with a prayer about the mouth and tongue?
questions.answer: The final verse turns the teaching into a request for restraint: a watch over the mouth and a seal upon the lips. After warnings about ill-timed conversation, insults, secrets, and friendship, the speaker recognizes that speech can cause his own fall. The chapter closes by treating wise speech as something that must be guarded.

glossary.def: A lazy or inactive person, described in verses 1-2 through images of defilement and filth to show public disgrace.
A person lacking wisdom or understanding; in this chapter the fool resists instruction and becomes a lasting burden to others.
Practical discernment or grasp of wisdom; the chapter says the fool lacks it and contrasts it with thoughtful stability.
The repair of a damaged friendship; verse 22 says it may be possible after harmful speech, except where betrayal or serious insult has driven the friend away.
An image for guarded, wise restraint placed upon the lips so that the speaker's tongue does not destroy him.
